caption: Figure 1. Overview of the MASPO Framework. The optimization proceeds sequentially following the topological order of the agent
text_block: We present MASPO, a framework designed to navigate the non-stationary and combinatorial landscape of multi-agent prompt optimization. As illustrated in Figure 1, our work- flow follows a systematic loop: it orchestrates agents via a topological protocol, generates candidates through trace analysis, evaluates them using a multi-granularity reward, and evolves the population via an adaptive beam search.
title: MASPO: Joint Prompt Optimization for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
visual_description:
1. The figure, titled “MASPO: Joint Prompt Optimization for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems,” presents an end-to-end architecture with four main regions. The upper-left blue region contains an LLM evaluator and a prompt optimizer; the upper-right pink region is the target multi-agent system; the lower-left blue region identifies misalignment cases, computes joint rewards, and constructs a search tree; and the lower-right green region performs “Trace-Guided Beam Search” and returns the best prompt.

2. In the upper-left evaluation region, the model \(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{eval}}\), shown as an evaluator robot, assesses behavior at three granularities. The “Local-level” block contains one agent, the “Lookahead-level” block contains a short interaction between two agents, and the “Global-level” block contains a larger four-agent configuration. Thick branching connectors associate \(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{eval}}\) with all three evaluation levels.

3. The prompt optimizer sends a pair of prompts \(p,p'\) leftward toward the three-level evaluation structure. The resulting outputs are compared in a block labeled \(o\ \mathrm{vs.}\ o'\), reached by a downward arrow from \(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{eval}}\). This comparison determines whether the original and candidate prompts align at the local, lookahead, and global levels.

4. The cream-colored “Prompt Optimizer” contains an optimization model \(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{opt}}\). A right-pointing arrow labeled “Generating” leads from \(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{opt}}\) to a candidate-prompt set represented by multiple nodes and labeled
\[
\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{cand}}=\{p'_1,p'_2,\ldots\}.
\]
Thus, the optimizer generates multiple candidate revisions of the current prompt.

5. Below the optimizer is a sample bank labeled “Samples \(\mathcal{B}_{iter}\cup\mathcal{B}_{mis}\).” An upward arrow labeled “Query \(q\)” supplies a query to the prompt optimizer. A right-pointing arrow labeled “Prompt \(p\)” sends a sampled prompt to an executing agent. The multi-agent system supplies “Context \(\mathcal{C}\)” to that agent through a left-pointing connector, and the agent’s “Output \(o\)” is returned upward to the prompt optimizer.

6. The upper-right multi-agent-system region contains five prompt-bearing agent nodes labeled \(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4,\) and \(p_5\). Their directed communication graph includes arrows \(p_1\rightarrow p_3\), \(p_1\rightarrow p_2\), \(p_3\rightarrow p_2\), \(p_3\rightarrow p_4\), \(p_2\rightarrow p_4\), \(p_2\rightarrow p_5\), and \(p_4\rightarrow p_5\). The text “Prompt \(p_1\)” identifies the prompt assigned to the leftmost agent. A lower strip depicts the corresponding multi-agent interaction sequence as several agents connected from left to right, followed by an ellipsis.

7. A large downward blue arrow from the \(o\) versus \(o'\) comparison leads to the lower-left “Misalignment Case” block. The illustrated case has a correct original local output \(o_{loc}\) and an incorrect revised local output \(o'_{loc}\). Below a dashed divider, the conjunction shows incorrect original lookahead and global outputs, \(o_{look}\) and \(o_{glob}\), but correct revised outputs \(o'_{look}\) and \(o'_{glob}\). Green checks denote alignment or correctness, while red crosses denote misalignment. This criterion is labeled “Eq.(6).”

8. A right-pointing arrow from the misalignment block leads to the condition
\[
\mathcal{B}_{mis}\subseteq\mathcal{B}_{iter},\qquad
|\mathcal{B}_{mis}|<K_{mis}.
\]
This states that the misalignment subset is drawn from the iterative sample set and is limited to fewer than \(K_{mis}\) samples. The resulting \(\mathcal{B}_{iter}\cup\mathcal{B}_{mis}\) is fed upward into the sample bank used by the prompt optimizer.

9. The “Joint Reward Model” combines three evaluation rewards with weights \(\alpha,\beta,\theta\):
\[
\sum
\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha\cdot R_{loc}\\
\beta\cdot R_{look}\\
\theta\cdot R_{glob}
\end{pmatrix}
=
R(p',p;\mathcal{B}_{iter}).
\]
The formula is labeled “Eq.(5).” Its output is sent rightward to the prompt-search procedure.

10. The “Construct Search Tree” block represents the current prompt \(p\) as a blue root node and candidate prompts \(p'_1,p'_2,p'_3\) as yellow child nodes. Solid branches connect the root to candidates, with one visible branch score of \(0.6\); dashed branches indicate additional candidate relations. A large right-pointing blue arrow transfers this candidate tree to the trace-guided beam-search region.

11. In “Trace-Guided Beam Search,” the root prompt \(p\) branches to \(p'_1\) with score \(0.5\) and \(p'_2\) with score \(0.6\). At the next depth, \(p'_1\) branches to \(p''_1\) with score \(0.1\) and \(p''_2\) with score \(0.6\), while \(p'_2\) branches to \(p''_3\) with score \(0.4\) and \(p''_4\) with score \(0.8\). These second-level candidates are enclosed in a box labeled “TopK.” Green nodes are retained candidates and red nodes are pruned candidates.

12. The retained node \(p''_2\) branches to \(p'''_1\) with score \(0.8\) and \(p'''_2\) with score \(0.3\). The retained node \(p''_4\) branches to \(p'''_3\) with score \(0.2\) and \(p'''_4\) with score \(0.7\). The two displayed cumulative trace scores are
\[
0.5+0.6+0.8=1.9
\]
and
\[
0.6+0.8+0.7=2.1.
\]
The second trace has the larger total, so its terminal candidate \(p'''_4\) is selected.

13. The selected route is labeled \(p_{\mathrm{best}}\) in green and is connected to a vertical multi-agent execution strip on the right. This strip shows a sequence of agents joined by downward arrows, with the first agent marked by a green check and an ellipsis indicating continuation. The selected best prompt is thereby returned to the multi-agent system for the next optimization iteration.
